s01: What if your delivery methodology didn't live in documents, but ran inside the work?
AI in Delivery, at a New Zealand bank.
s02: People orchestrate the work, and agents and skills do the heavy lifting, in discovery and in development.
At every step, the agents check their work against nCino's own knowledge, through the nCino MCP.
People review the outputs twice, at discovery and again at code. Only then do the agents execute the remaining tasks.
And it's Accenture people, with the skills, who make the efficiency real.
Grounded in nCino. Decided by people. Delivered by Accenture.
s03: One feature. Morning in Wellington, afternoon in Manila.
s04: It's morning in Wellington. A functional consultant opens the feature page for a new business lending product.
It was signed off weeks ago, but the system has changed since.
So her first question isn't what to build. It's what is still true.
She runs the Refinement and Reconcile agent. It reads the earlier pages, the policy rules, and a snapshot of how nCino is set up today.
Every claim it makes points to a source. No path, no claim.
s05: The agent comes back with a process map, and two open questions.
The first is a gap in the requirement. No exception path is defined for the new product, so it goes to the business analyst.
The second is a possible known issue in the platform itself. That one goes to nCino's professional services team. It's never assumed.
Each question gets an owner, and a three day clock.
The agent found them. She decided they were real.
s06: Next, the Story Writer turns the requirements into three stories, in plain business language.
Every acceptance criterion cites the rule it came from.
The story that depends on the open questions stays in draft.
The Task Decomposer breaks the other two into tasks precise enough to start. Where a fact is missing, the task carries the question, not a guess.
She adjusts one task, and approves. The Publisher puts it all on the board, linked back to the feature page.
s08: A developer opens Claude Code. The health check clears, and his ticket arrives with its story, its criteria, and its lineage. No copy and paste.
This is a flow change, so the agent maps the impact first: three callers, and one link into another domain.
Until that map exists, the edit is blocked. A guard enforces it, not a reviewer's memory.
He builds in a cloned dev org. The change is checked against nCino's own guidance, then validated against the sandbox.
The unit test gate finds one missing assertion. The agent fixes it, and the gate goes green.
The gate blocks. It never softens on a second try.
Then the QA Plan agent writes the test plan, and hands it to the tester.
s09: He raises the pull request. It tells the reviewer what to look at first, and what could go wrong.
The automated checks all pass. But nothing merges by machine. A named reviewer approves.
A short retro captures one lesson. Hit it twice, and it becomes a skill or a gate.
It's twenty past five in Manila.
s10: One month in, the information is at the programme's fingertips, and the delivery pod is shaped around it.
Measured sprint against sprint, with AI on and off, the squad completed about three times as many tickets, with stories the same size and the same people.
That three times is two good stories. About twice as many user stories were delivered, and the squad cleared a backlog of older bugs, while fixing new ones in the same sprint they were raised.
Nothing was carried forward, and problems are now found close to where they are made.
Every developer is held to one standard, and every design builds on what nCino already provides.
It's a reusable model, trained into the squad in nine weeks, and packaged up as an asset, ready to be deployed.
s11: Agents draft. People decide. Nothing merges by machine.
